headline: New $500M Alliance Focuses on Saving Earth's Most Endangered Species
meta_description: The Bezos Earth Fund and eight partners pledge $500 million to help rescue threatened plants and animals, shifting conservation focus to species recovery.
summary_short: A new alliance backed by the Bezos Earth Fund commits $500 million over five years to help save critically endangered species worldwide.
body:
Nine organizations, led by the Bezos Earth Fund, have committed more than $500 million over five years to rescue some of the planet's most threatened plants and animals. The Species Recovery Alliance, announced in October at the United Nations biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, represents a significant shift in global conservation funding—moving beyond protected areas to focus directly on helping endangered species recover. The alliance will coordinate investments and support recovery projects through conservation organizations and local partners, rather than creating a single pooled fund. About a third of the $500 million represents new financing, according to Cristián Samper, managing director at the Bezos Earth Fund.

The initiative builds on urgent need. Wildlife populations globally have collapsed: vertebrate wildlife populations declined by an average of 73 percent between 1970 and 2022, with Africa experiencing an 80 percent decline, according to the WWF's 2026 Living Planet Report. "We're forgetting some of the other targets, in particular, the Target 4 on recovery of endangered species," Samper explained, referring to the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

The alliance includes Re:wild, Rainforest Trust, Fondation Segré, and five other organizations. Its members will work with local conservation groups to intervene directly in the recovery of threatened species, recognizing that protected areas alone are insufficient. The commitment builds on the Bezos Earth Fund's Phoenix Species Project, launched in August to support the recovery of 100 critically endangered species across 30 countries. Success will be measured using indicators developed by the IUCN, the global wildlife conservation authority. Samper acknowledged that results could take decades for slow-breeding species, but expressed hope that focused effort, proper capacity, and additional resources could help reverse the tide of extinction.
quick_facts: $500 million pledged by Bezos Earth Fund and eight partner organizations
Announced at UN biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia in October
73% decline in vertebrate wildlife populations between 1970 and 2022
Targets recovery of 100 critically endangered species across 30 countries
About one-third of funding represents new money
